faq.title: Will migrating to a new Mastodon server transfer my past toots and posts?
faq.description: No. The W3C ActivityPub Move activity strictly migrates your follower connections, following list, mutes, and blocks. It does NOT transfer your past posts to the new server because each post is permanently addressed to the URL of the originating instance. You can, however, export an archive of your past posts for personal backup.

faq.title: How long does a Mastodon follower migration take to complete?
faq.description: Follower migration depends on the number of followers you have and the responsiveness of remote Fediverse instances. When your old server broadcasts the 'Move' activity, thousands of remote instances must verify the cryptographic HTTP signature and update their local database inboxes. For a few thousand followers, the process typically takes between 2 to 24 hours.

faq.title: Can I migrate back to my old Mastodon server if I change my mind?
faq.description: Mastodon enforces a mandatory 30-day cooldown period following an account migration to prevent malicious server spam and bouncing attacks. Once you initiate a move, you cannot migrate that account again for 30 days.

html:
The Fediverse, powered by the W3C ActivityPub open standard, represents the largest federated alternative to centralized Big Tech social networks. In the Fediverse, independent servers run by universities, nonprofit cooperatives, and passionate individuals communicate over standardized JSON-LD protocols. However, because individual servers are privately funded and operated, instances occasionally shut down, run out of storage, or enforce moderation rules that conflict with an individual's personal ethics.

Fortunately, ActivityPub was engineered with Identity Portability in mind. Mastodon provides a built-in cryptographic migration workflow that allows you to pack up your social graph and move to a new server without losing your followers. Understanding the underlying protocol mechanics of ActivityPub Actor objects, RSA HTTP signatures, and Move activities ensures a seamless transition without orphan accounts or broken federation links.

The ActivityPub Protocol: How Fediverse Identity Works

In ActivityPub, every user account is represented as an Actor Object—a JSON-LD document accessible over HTTPS. A typical Mastodon Actor document contains:

  • id: The canonical URI representing the account (e.g., https://mastodon.social/users/alice).
  • inbox: The server endpoint where other Fediverse instances deliver replies, mentions, and follow requests.
  • outbox: The public endpoint where the user's published activities (posts, boosts) are streamed.
  • publicKey: An RSA-2048 public cryptographic key used to authenticate all outbound activities via HTTP Signatures.
  • alsoKnownAs: An array of URIs linking the actor to alternative identities across the Fediverse.

The Mechanics of the Move Activity

Migrating followers from an old instance (server-A.com) to a new instance (server-B.com) is a two-way cryptographic handshake governed by the ActivityPub Move Activity:

  1. Alias Establishment: You create a new account on server-B.com and add an alsoKnownAs property pointing to your old account on server-A.com. This proves to the world that you authorize the connection.
  2. Migration Trigger: You log into server-A.com and initiate the account redirect, providing the handle of the new account.
  3. Cryptographic Move Broadcast: server-A.com synthesizes an ActivityPub Move activity payload: 
    {
  "@context": "https://www.w3.org/ns/activitystreams",
  "id": "https://server-a.com/activities/move-123",
  "type": "Move",
  "actor": "https://server-a.com/users/alice",
  "object": "https://server-a.com/users/alice",
  "target": "https://server-b.com/users/alice"
}
  4. server-A.com signs this payload using Alice's old private RSA key and blasts it to the sharedInbox endpoints of every remote server where Alice's followers reside.
  5. Remote Follower Re-Routing: When remote servers (e.g., pixelfed.social or techhub.social) receive the signed Move activity, their Sidekiq background workers verify the cryptographic signature against Alice's old public key, confirm the reciprocal alsoKnownAs link on server-B.com, and automatically update their local database so their local users are now following https://server-b.com/users/alice!

Step-by-Step Mastodon Migration Guide

To successfully migrate your Mastodon account without dropping followers, follow this exact sequence:

Phase 1: Create and Prepare the New Account

  1. Register an account on your new target Mastodon server (e.g., https://fosstodon.org).
  2. Complete your profile setup (avatar, bio, display name).
  3. Navigate to Preferences > Account > Moving from a different account.
  4. Click create an account alias.
  5. Enter your old account's handle (e.g., alice@mastodon.social) and click Save Alias. This step is critical; without it, the old server will refuse to broadcast the Move activity!

Phase 2: Export Data from the Old Account

  1. Log into your old Mastodon instance.
  2. Navigate to Preferences > Import and Export > Data Export.
  3. Download CSV files for: Following list, Lists, Mutes, Blocks, and Bookmarks.
  4. (Optional) Request your full post archive for permanent offline archival.

Phase 3: Import Relationships into the New Account

  1. Return to your new account on the new server.
  2. Navigate to Preferences > Import and Export > Import.
  3. Select Following list, upload your CSV file, choose Merge, and submit. Repeat for blocks and mutes.

Phase 4: Execute the Follower Migration

  1. Return to your old Mastodon account.
  2. Navigate to Preferences > Account > Move to a different account.
  3. Click Configure it here.
  4. Enter your new account handle (e.g., alice@fosstodon.org) and confirm with your account password.
  5. Click Move Followers. Your old account profile will immediately display a redirect notice, and background federation workers will begin migrating your followers to the new server.

Sidekiq Worker Pipelines and Fediverse Delivery Queues

Under the hood, a production Mastodon server is an asynchronous, high-throughput distributed system written in Ruby on Rails, backed by PostgreSQL, Redis, and Sidekiq background job queues. Understanding how Sidekiq delivers ActivityPub messages explains why follower migrations and federated boosts behave the way they do:

  • The Ingress Pipeline: When a remote server sends an ActivityPub JSON payload to your server's /inbox, the web server (Puma) does not process the post immediately. It writes the raw payload to Redis and pushes a job onto the default Sidekiq worker queue, immediately returning an HTTP 202 Accepted response.
  • Cryptographic Verification Workers: Sidekiq workers fetch the remote actor's public RSA key (caching it locally in PostgreSQL), verify the incoming HTTP Signature against the message digest, and parse the activity.
  • Fan-Out on Delivery: When you broadcast a post or an account Move activity, your server's push Sidekiq queue splits the delivery into hundreds of parallel jobs—one for every unique sharedInbox domain across your followers' instances. If a remote server is offline or experiencing heavy load, Sidekiq automatically retries delivery with exponential backoff over a 72-hour window.

Instance Defederation, Silence, and Domain Block Propagation

Unlike centralized platforms where corporate trust-and-safety committees unilaterally ban users, moderation on Mastodon occurs at the Instance Level:

  1. Domain Silencing: An instance administrator can mark a remote domain as "Silenced." When silenced, posts from that server remain accessible via direct search, but are hidden from the public federated timeline and notifications are suppressed for local users.
  2. Domain Suspending (Defederation): Complete severance of federation links. When two instances defederate, all existing follower relationships between those instances are permanently severed, past cached media is deleted from local disk storage, and incoming/outbound HTTP signatures are dropped at the Nginx reverse proxy layer.
  3. Impact on Migration: If you migrate your account to a server that is widely defederated by other large communities, followers residing on those defederated servers will be unable to receive your Move activity, effectively stranding your social graph! Always audit an instance's public moderation blocklist before choosing it as your new home.

Self-Hosting: Redis Caching and Media S3 Object Storage Optimization

Operating a federated Mastodon instance requires strict infrastructure resource management:

  • S3-Compatible Object Storage: Never store user-uploaded media (photos, video clips, custom emojis) on local server SSDs. Configure Mastodon to stream media directly to Cloudflare R2, Wasabi, or Amazon S3 to prevent disk exhaustion.
  • PostgreSQL Vacuuming and Index Maintenance: The statuses and account_pins tables accumulate millions of foreign database records rapidly. Running scheduled cron jobs for tootctl media remove and database index vacuuming is mandatory to maintain sub-100ms response times.
  • Streaming API Node Process: Mastodon runs a dedicated Node.js WebSocket service (mastodon-streaming) that streams live timeline updates and direct notifications to active web and mobile clients without polling the Ruby on Rails backend.

Handling Cross-Instance Account Alias Verification Pitfalls

When executing an account migration, administrators and users frequently encounter edge-case failure modes:

  1. DNS Caching Inconsistencies: If your new instance recently changed IP addresses or updated TLS certificates, remote servers with cached DNS records may fail to verify the alsoKnownAs URI, causing the Move activity to be rejected silently. Always ensure TTLs are lowered 24 hours prior to migration.
  2. Rate-Limiting on Inboxes: Massive instances (like mastodon.social) enforce strict rate-limits on incoming HTTP POST requests to prevent denial-of-service floods. If you have 50,000 followers, your instance's Sidekiq workers must throttle deliveries to stay beneath remote API rate-limit thresholds.

ActivityPub JSON-LD Serialization and Signature Verification Benchmarks

ActivityPub messages rely heavily on JSON-LD (Linked Data) compaction and expansion algorithms. Each HTTP request requires computing a cryptographic digest over the HTTP request target, date header, host, and body:

(request-target): post /inbox
host: target-instance.org
date: Sat, 28 Nov 2026 10:00:00 GMT
digest: SHA-256=X48E9qOokqqrvdts8nOJRJN3OWDUoyWxBf7kbu9DBPE=

For high-traffic instances handling 10,000 requests per second, performing RSA-2048 verification on every single incoming JSON-LD request becomes a massive CPU bottleneck. Modern instance administrators deploy Nginx reverse proxies with OpenSSL hardware acceleration or transition to Ed25519 signatures, slashing signature verification latency by up to 80%.

Backing Up and Restoring Post Archives Offline

Because the Move activity intentionally excludes status posts, preserving your personal writing requires manual backup extraction. Mastodon exports archives as a tar.gz bundle containing an outbox.json ActivityStreams document alongside all uploaded media attachments. You can host this static archive on GitHub Pages, Cloudflare Pages, or a personal static website as an immutable, search-indexed personal writing portfolio!

Custom Server Rules and Defederation Appeal Workflows

In the decentralized Fediverse, each server establishes its own Terms of Service and Code of Conduct. If your instance is silenced or defederated by peer servers due to administrative disagreements or rogue user activity, you may find your posts isolated from the broader network. Active server administrators monitor Fediverse defederation registries (like FediCheck and Fediverse Blocklists) and maintain bilateral communication channels with peer moderators to resolve dispute escalations and restore cross-server federation links. Proactive community communication and clear server moderation guidelines remain the foundation of healthy federated communities.
